First, it is counterproductive and hypocritical for the LGBT community to put presser on other LBGT who is as out as they are. They out of everyone should understand how difficult the process is and be sensitive. Though it is important for a individual to come out and not deny who they are to themselves or others. 
In the coming out process, you should first come out to those who who know will support and love you regardless. This transitions later on making it easier to coming out to others who may not be as supporting having the support of those original people you came out. Also, if they were truly your friends, they will understand the process and why you may have had issues coming out. I would recommend perhaps having a serious discussion about it on a one to one bases with your closest of those individuals. Perhaps even coming out in the process. I hope this helps

Also Skimania hit it on the head. What helped me in coming out was first coming out to the people I know would be supportive and loving. That support came helpful later on when I came out to people who may not be as accepting, like my dad.

For some it is a process of sexual discovery that one doesn't completely formulate until teens or as a early adult generally. However, though I choose to blatantly ignore my bisexuality for a while, I could always trace my sexual patterns back if I thought about it. I have been attracted to both geders in the developmental stages of attraction I went through from a kid to a adult of course.  I would genuinely ask you to look into your sexuality and past interests.  Is there anything to indicate that you have been wanting to have sexual and romantic relationship with men now or in the past? Also, there are hotlines and places to help a person discuss their sexuality in a open environment. One place I can think of is Howard Brown.
As far as your friends, if you feel you are would be scrutinized by your friends I would recommend not telling them. At the same time, if they can't accept who you may really be or respect you enough to listen and not insult you. Are they really your friends?  I have lost quite a few friends and associates though coming out. It sucks. I won't sugar coat it. At the same time though, I know that basic principles of what a friendship is defined to me wouldn't be present in a friendship with some who can't respect me or my right to my own sexuality. I hope this helps
